title: Tuning hydrogen desorption through biaxial strain in Li- and Na-based perovskite hydrides
content: The structural, hydrogen-storage, mechanical, thermodynamic, electronic and optical properties of the cubic perovskite-type hydrides AeXH3 (Ae = Li, Na; X = Sc, Ti, V; Pm3̄m, no. 221) were investigated by first-principles density-functional theory within the generalized-gradient approximation. The lattice parameters decrease systematically from Sc to V, reflecting contraction of the metal–hydrogen framework. The gravimetric hydrogen capacities are 5.51, 5.23 and 4.96 wt% for LiScH3, LiTiH3 and LiVH3, and 3.93–4.26 wt% for the sodium analogues. Negative formation enthalpies indicate favourable formation from the elements, with LiVH3 the most negative (−4.15 eV per atom). For the non-magnetic cells, referred to the AeXH reduced phase, the estimated desorption temperatures range from 285.94 to 1424.81 K, with LiVH3 the lowest. Biaxial strain (−6% to +6%) lowers both the magnitude of the formation enthalpy and the desorption temperature, offering a practical route to facilitate hydrogen release. The elastic constants satisfy the Born stability criteria, and Cauchy pressures and Pugh ratios indicate predominantly brittle behaviour. Debye temperatures increase from Sc to V, consistent with the stiffening X–H framework. The non-magnetic band structures and densities of states show metallic character arising from H s–transition-metal d hybridization, and the optical spectra show strong ultraviolet absorption and conductivity. Spin-polarised Quantum ESPRESSO calculations with the D3 dispersion correction show that the Sc compounds remain non-magnetic, whereas LiTiH3 and NaTiH3 order as C-type and LiVH3 and NaVH3 as G-type antiferromagnets, lying 39–117 and 784–1004 meV per formula unit below the non-magnetic state; this order persists under biaxial strain from −6% to +6%. Relative to the elements and molecular H2, the formation enthalpies of the magnetic ground states lie between −48.6 and −113.9 kJ mol−1 H2, and magnetism contributes 43–70 kJ mol−1 H2 of the binding in the V hydrides. Overall, the Li-based hydrides, especially LiScH3 and LiTiH3, emerge as promising solid-state hydrogen-storage candidates, and the magnetic state of the Ti and V compounds must be considered when estimating their stability and desorption temperature.
